lead: A microprocessor is a whole CPU on one chip: it can add, compare and decide, but it cannot store a program or drive a motor alone. A microcontroller is that CPU plus program memory, working memory, timers and input/output pins on the same chip. The first suits computing power; the second suits a cheap, small, low-power chip controlling one device — a washing machine, an energy meter, a traffic light.
prereq: You need: the ALU from 5.2, the adder from 5.4, bus selection from 5.5, and registers from 5.6.

sections.h3: The microprocessor: a CPU on one chip

blocks.text: A microprocessor is a single silicon chip holding the central processing unit (CPU) of a computer. It fetches instructions, does arithmetic and makes decisions, and contains nothing else. Program memory, data memory, timers and input/output circuits sit on other chips, wired to it. The 8085 and 8086 are early examples; the processor in a laptop is the same idea built larger.

items: ALU (arithmetic logic unit): adds, subtracts, ANDs, ORs and compares, built from the gates of 5.2 and the adder of 5.4.
Register file: fast storage cells (5.6) holding the numbers being worked on now.
Program counter (PC): address of the next instruction to be fetched.
Instruction register (IR): the instruction being decoded now.
Control unit: switches the other blocks on in the right order.
Address bus: one-way; with n lines it selects 2ⁿ memory locations.
Data bus: two-way, carries numbers in and out.
Control bus: carries read/write, clock and interrupt signals.
Fetch: the control unit puts the PC value on the address bus, reads the byte stored there into the IR, and increments the PC.
Decode: the control unit works out what the instruction means and which registers and ALU operation it needs.
Execute: operands are read, the ALU or a register does the work, the result is written back.
Repeat from step 1.

blocks.where: t is the time for one instruction in seconds, CPI is the average number of clock cycles that instruction needs (a pure number), f is the clock frequency in hertz.

blocks.text: Word length is the number of bits the ALU handles at a time: 8 bits for an 8-bit chip, 32 for a 32-bit chip. It usually, not always, matches the data bus width — the 8088 has a 16-bit word and an 8-bit data bus. It sets the largest number the CPU can handle in one operation.

sections.h3: The microcontroller: the whole computer on one chip

blocks.text: A microcontroller (MCU) is a microprocessor plus the support circuits it needs, all on one chip. That is why one small package can run a whole appliance with no extra chips.

items: Flash or ROM program memory: keeps the program after power is removed.
RAM: working data; it loses its contents when power goes.
Timers and counters: count clock pulses to make delays or count events.
ADC (analog-to-digital converter): turns a sensor voltage into a number; many microcontrollers have it on chip, but the classic 8051 needs an external ADC0808 read through a port.
UART (universal asynchronous receiver-transmitter), a serial port: sends and receives characters, for example to a PC.
GPIO (general purpose input/output) pins: digital pins set by software to drive a relay, LED or transistor, or read a switch.

blocks.text: Two one-line comparisons. Von Neumann architecture uses one memory for program and data; Harvard architecture has separate program and data memories, so both can be read at once. CISC (complex instruction set computer) offers many powerful instructions; RISC (reduced instruction set computer) offers few simple, fast ones.

The 8051 family is the standard teaching chip: 8-bit CPU, 4 KB on-chip program memory, 128 bytes RAM, 32 input/output pins as four 8-bit ports, and two 16-bit timers. One timer counts from 0 to 65535 and overflows, so a longer delay is made by counting overflows.

An embedded system is a computer built inside a product to control that product, not to be a general-purpose computer. It runs one fixed program, usually forever, and its user never sees an operating system. A microcontroller is its typical heart.

items: Washing machine: reads the water-level sensor through the ADC, runs the motor for a set time using a timer, drives relays and LEDs from GPIO pins.
Microwave oven: timer for the cooking period, GPIO for the door switch, magnetron relay and display.
Air-conditioner: reads a temperature sensor, compares it with the set value, switches the compressor through a relay.
Car engine control: reads sensors and fires the fuel injector at the exact instant using timers.
Energy meter: counts pulses proportional to energy, keeps the total in memory, sends it over the serial port.
Traffic light: a timer drives the red, yellow and green lamps in sequence.

blocks.text: The choice is the same each time. If the job needs a keyboard, a screen and a large program, use a microprocessor with separate memory. If the job is to sense, time and switch a few loads, use a microcontroller: one chip, fewer wires, lower cost, lower power.

spec.title: Inside a microcontroller chip
spec.aria: A single chip drawn as a system bus with seven blocks: CPU core, Flash, RAM, timers, ADC, GPIO and UART. In a Harvard part Flash and RAM use separate buses; this single bus is the simplified von Neumann view.

examples.question: A washing machine controller must read a water-level sensor whose output is an analog voltage, run the motor for 5 minutes, light an LED when the cycle ends, and sound a buzzer. The controller uses an 8051-family chip: 8-bit CPU, 4 KB program memory, 128 bytes RAM, two 16-bit timers, 32 input/output pins, and a 12 MHz crystal with 12 clock cycles per machine cycle. The program is 3.5 KB. The variables are: water level 1 byte, two 16-bit timer counts (2 bytes each), flags 1 byte. Four pins are used. Find the free program memory in bytes, the free RAM in bytes, the free I/O pins, and the number of 16-bit timer overflows needed for the 5-minute run. Then say whether a microprocessor or a microcontroller is the right choice.
steps: Blocks needed: an ADC input for the analog sensor (on-chip on ADC-equipped variants, otherwise an external ADC0808 read through a port), a timer for the 5-minute run, GPIO outputs for the motor relay, LED and buzzer, and program memory and RAM.
Program memory: 3.5 KB = 3.5 × 1024 = 3584 bytes. Flash 4096 bytes. Free = 4096 − 3584 = 512 bytes.
Pins used: motor relay, LED, buzzer = 3 outputs; sensor input = 1; total 4. Free = 32 − 4 = 28 pins.
Timer resolution: 12 MHz ÷ 12 = 1 MHz machine cycle, so 1 count = 1 µs.
Run time: 5 minutes = 300 s = 300 × 10⁶ µs = 300,000,000 counts.
One 16-bit timer counts 65536 before overflowing. Overflows = 300,000,000 ÷ 65536 = 4577.64, so 4578 overflows (the last is partial).

Decision: timer, GPIO, program memory and RAM are on chip; only the ADC is outside (built in on ADC-equipped variants), so a microcontroller is still right. A microprocessor would need separate ROM, RAM, timer and ADC chips plus more wiring.
examples.answer: Free program memory 512 bytes, free RAM 122 bytes, free I/O pins 28, and 4578 timer overflows for the 5-minute run; a microcontroller such as the 8051 family is the right choice.
examples.check:
import math
flash = 4 * 1024
program = 3.5 * 1024
print(int(flash - program))
ram_used = 1 + 2 + 2 + 1
print(128 - ram_used)
print(32 - 4)
counts = 300 * 10**6
print(math.ceil(counts / 65536))

traps: Swapping the definitions: a microprocessor does not have RAM, timers or GPIO on chip; a microcontroller has its own program memory.
Judging a chip by clock speed alone: time per instruction is CPI ÷ f, so a 16 MHz chip needing 4 cycles per instruction can be slower than an 8 MHz chip needing 1.
Confusing the address bus with the data bus: n address lines give 2ⁿ locations; the data bus carries data, and its width usually but not always equals the word length.
Calling the 8051's 4 KB program memory ‘RAM’: the 4 KB is Flash/ROM for the program and only 128 bytes are RAM.
Thinking the 8051 timer counts seconds: it counts machine cycles, so divide the crystal frequency by 12 to get the count rate.

quiz.q: What does the program counter (PC) hold?
quiz.a: The address of the next instruction to be fetched from program memory.

quiz.q: State the 8051's program memory size, RAM size and number of input/output pins.
quiz.a: 4 KB program memory, 128 bytes RAM, 32 input/output pins.

quiz.q: Why does a microprocessor need extra chips around it to run a washing machine?
quiz.a: It contains only the CPU: ALU, registers, PC, IR, control unit and buses. It has no program memory, RAM, timer, ADC or general-purpose input/output ports; parallel I/O must come from an external chip such as the 8255, wired to the processor's bus. A microcontroller already has these on chip.

quiz.q: Give one difference between von Neumann and Harvard architecture, and one between CISC and RISC.
quiz.a: Von Neumann uses one memory for program and data; Harvard uses separate program and data memories. CISC has many complex instructions; RISC has few simple instructions that execute fast.

quiz.q: An 8051 runs from a 12 MHz crystal with 12 clocks per machine cycle. A motor must run for 3 minutes. How many 16-bit timer overflows are needed?
quiz.a: 1 count = 1 µs. 3 minutes = 180 s = 180 × 10⁶ µs. One timer counts 65536 before overflow. 180,000,000 ÷ 65536 = 2746.58, so 2747 overflows.

quiz.q: A chip has a 16-line address bus and an 8-bit data bus. How many memory locations can it address, and how many bits does the ALU handle per operation if the word length is 8 bits?
quiz.a: 2¹⁶ = 65536 locations; the ALU handles 8 bits per operation.

quiz.q: Two microcontrollers are offered: 16 MHz with 4 cycles per instruction, and 8 MHz with 1 cycle per instruction. Which finishes a 1000-instruction loop first? Show the times.
quiz.a: First: t = 1000 × 4 ÷ (16 × 10⁶) = 250 µs. Second: t = 1000 × 1 ÷ (8 × 10⁶) = 125 µs. The slower-clocked 8 MHz chip finishes first, because clock speed alone does not fix the work done.

quiz.q: A traffic light must hold each lamp for 30 s, drive three lamp relays and be reprogrammed on site. Which blocks of a microcontroller are used, and why is a microprocessor a poor fit?
quiz.a: A timer for the 30 s delay, three GPIO output pins for the lamp relays, and Flash program memory for the stored sequence. A microprocessor would need external ROM, RAM, timer and I/O chips, giving a larger, costlier, more power-hungry board for a job needing only a few pins and one fixed program.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real products mostly use 32-bit ARM Cortex-M or RISC-V microcontrollers; Wi-Fi chips such as the ESP32 add a radio to the same die. Firmware is written in C and scheduled by a real-time operating system (RTOS) when tasks share the CPU. Low-power design, interrupt latency and watchdog timers become key. Search for ‘ARM Cortex-M architecture’, ‘RISC-V microcontroller’, ‘RTOS task scheduling’ and ‘embedded C GPIO register’.
